html:
The Massachusett were an Algonquian people of the coast around Massachusetts Bay, where Boston stands today. Their name means "at the great hill", likely the Blue Hills south of the bay. They farmed maize, beans and squash, fished and gathered shellfish, and moved between summer and winter villages.

An epidemic brought by European sailors swept the New England coast from 1616 to 1619 and killed most of them. When the English of the Puritan migration arrived in 1630, they found cleared fields and few people, and named their Massachusetts Bay colony after the Massachusett.

The missionary John Eliot learned their language and printed a whole Bible in it in 1663, the Eliot Indian Bible. Christian converts lived in "praying towns" such as Natick. Many were interned or killed during King Philip's War in 1675 and 1676. Their neighbours were the Wampanoag, the Nipmuc and the Pawtucket. The same people appear on later maps as Massachusett.
